title: ROMS: iOS server manager app with multi-snippets/SSH/Shortcuts (TestFlight)
summary:
Hi, I’m working on ROMS (Run It On My Server), an SSH app for connecting to and managing remote servers from Apple devices.

I built this app to manage my server quickly from my iPhone or iPad.

ROMS includes an interactive terminal, reusable snippets for commands you run often and multi-snippets for running commands across multiple servers.

It also integrates with Apple Shortcuts, so you can run a snippet or multi-snippet and see the output in the Shortcuts sheet.

You can organize servers with tags and keep your most-used servers and snippets in Favorites.

The terminal is also customizable: you can choose fonts, sizes, and colors, and edit the terminal toolbar by adding, removing, and rearranging keys. ROMS also supports iCloud sync and backup/export for your settings, servers, and snippets.

Here's a video: https://streamable.com/o1axb0

title: How to Stay Abreast of Compromised Software?
summary:
Especially as I've been using AI and churning through an order of magnitude more software on my computer, I've been wondering what best practices are to stay abreast of compromises, bad releases, hacked software, etc. I've been wondering what a reasonable duration of lagging behind updates is to allow for exploited software to be alerted by the community, while also updating quick enough that I don't let my system remain with known + fixed bugs. I anticipate the answer is partly: use less software, containerize/sandbox, and understand what I install. But that's not fun, not always possible for the multitude of applications I actually use to intentionally interface with my sensitive data, and not always possible due to time constraints.

What have you guys been doing to hedge against corrupted software? Anyone have any leads on where I could read deep dives from experts on this topic?

title: Four C/C++ libraries ported to pure managed .NET on a $20 plan
summary:
I'm between jobs right now, and I'm bad at sitting idle. I could have built yet another portfolio site with a chatbot and a smiling robot avatar, but I wanted to spend the time on something people might actually use.

There was a second reason. My feed is full of stories about LLM agents that burn thousands of dollars in tokens overnight. I suspected that most of them say more about the process than about the tools, and I wanted to check that on real work.

So over about three weeks, with Claude Code on a $20/month Pro plan as the main tool (plus $100 of promotional credits that were expiring anyway, and some free-tier model sessions for the routine parts), I ported four native libraries to fully managed C#, with no P/Invoke and no native binaries:

- Leptonica.Managed - Leptonica 1.87.0, image processing and the base of Tesseract OCR; about 2,700 functions. https://github.com/sensboston/Leptonica.Managed - Stb.Managed - seven of Sean Barrett's stb libraries (image load/save, resize, TrueType, rect_pack, DXT, Perlin). https://github.com/sensboston/Stb.Managed - MetadataSharp - EXIF/MakerNotes, IPTC, XMP and ICC read/write. Not a port: written from the specs, with Exiv2 as the reference. https://github.com/sensboston/MetadataSharp - MdfLibrary.Managed - mdflib, the ASAM MDF format of automotive data loggers, with the same API as its Windows-only C++/CLI wrapper, plus a cross-platform viewer with live CAN capture. https://github.com/sensboston/mdflib.net

All four are on NuGet under MIT.

I wouldn't call this vibe coding. The model wrote most of the code, but the work went the way any port of this size should go, with or without an LLM. First we discussed the architecture: what maps to what in C#, what stays bit-exact and what may be optimized, what is ported and what is left out. Then came a written plan in stages, each with a measurable exit condition. Before the first line of the port, the native library was built and became the oracle; the tests compare against it, not against the model's opinion of what the output should be. Then the work went in small batches, each merged only when CI was green.

The checks are boring on purpose: pixel by pixel against Leptonica's golden files, byte by byte against stb, tag by tag against exiv2 on its own test corpus, file by file against the native MdfLibrary. Parsers are fuzzed. It still isn't bulletproof: the GPU path of Stb.Managed passed every test on ILGPU's CPU accelerator and did not work at all on a real CUDA card. Tests are only as honest as the hardware they run on.

One result surprised me: the managed code is faster than C on most operations - about 1.3-2.0x single-threaded for Leptonica (regular Release build of the C library) and 1.5-1.8x for stb (-O3 -march=native). The JIT emits Vector128/256/512 code for the actual CPU, and Leptonica's C code has almost no SIMD. It is not faster everywhere: stb's hand-written SIMD resize still wins on one core, and JPEG on ARM64 is slower. The slow cases are listed in each repo.

Total extra cost beyond the subscription: $0. The expensive part was waiting for usage limits to reset; my patience turned out to be the scarcest resource in the project.

Happy to answer questions about the process, the verification, or the parts that went wrong.

title: I got $487 MRR in 3 days with zero ads. the exact distribution process I used
summary:
A few weeks ago I launched a product for accountant, to get easier the info of clients. No audience, no ad budget. no knowledge about accountant or similar arguments.

Here’s what actually i did to get this numbers (487 are low, but guys in 3 days is crazy i think):

1. Where I posted

sub-reddit, x, and linkedin. in first case, i try to give people real advice, and you know, try to get interest them in the thing. i don't want start the conversation: "i have problem x" and i reply "use my product"

it's not like this that the things works. So i created first of all interest, and in reality everything comes naturally. for X and Linkedin (Linkedin my fav) bascially i tryed to build something on me, in this case the topic building in public, helped me a lot, beacause i got: Engagment People People money That's all. Just keep consistent, and everything will arrive!

2. The post format that worked: like i said before, the topic building in public worked very good for me: "day 7 of building ... Today i improve the product and now it is faster, i need beta tester to test it out" cleary, it was longer and more specific, this is only a "type-post" that i used to do.

3. What I did with comments: for the first, i was like: ok, now with this comments? My Reddit posts have always performed quite well I’ve never run into any issues often ending up with 30 or more comments, leaving me wondering how to handle them. Because of this, I would try to spark a conversation (just as I mentioned earlier) by engaging potential customers and subtly bringing up the product. Honestly, it was very difficult to hold back from just saying, "Here’s the product go get it!" but I wasn't sure how the customer might react. More importantly, I wanted to avoid coming across as the typical founder who’s just hunting for customers.

4. What flopped: X. Actually, i expected much from X, but the clients are very low, and i think that i may close it now. a huge flop my guys.

Honestly the hardest part wasn’t any single tactic. It was knowing what to do each day and tracking what worked. I managed it all with messy spreadsheets and notes.

So I’m turning that process into a simple tool for solo founders: tells you where to post, what format to use, and what’s actually bringing signups.

If you’re struggling with distribution, drop your product below. I’ll suggest 2–3 places to start for free, and I’ll pick a few people to try the tool early.

title: Ask HN: Least cringe AI for natural language?
summary:
Just talked to Claude and couldn't believe how bad it was. Openly condescending! I used to prefer Claude because it was the most human-like (living up to the company name), but switched away a few months ago when they installed the "contemptuous British government official" personality.

ChatGPT still has the classic ChatGPT smell, but they've at least stayed very consistent with it (excepting GPT-5, of course).

On a more fundamental note, is anyone working with base/text models these days? I just saw that OpenAI's Davinci finally got retired a few weeks ago. Most of the OSS ones I found had synthetic cringe injected into the pretraining, so they weren't any good.

I don't think this is something you can prompt around -- at least in my experience, models disregard style prompts after the first turn...

Thoughts? Experiences? Would love to hear.

Thanks

title: Ask HN: Am I the only one whose AI hype is cooling down a lot?
summary:
I am in the industry for 15+ years, studied CS, and actually, never really "liked" programming. It was a means to an end. I have written about programming (and published books), so don't get me wrong: I like the craft and I miss the sense of accomplishment after hours and days of struggling and fixing a problem with 2 lines of code.

What I see in my personal spending and habits: I get free tokens from my company, and I spent between 3k-5k a month at the start of the year. Models got cheaper, but also: The usefullness ran its course a little bit for me.

I still don't write code by hand, but when doing research, finding solutions, even some decisions (using Opus 5.5 and Astra 6.2 for example) are more and more questionable. I handed large research tasks to models, but even small questions like: "What do you think about these PR comments pointing out issues" (I need to be vague, working for a larger company), it didn't find even basic facts I found via Google and reading the docs for 2mins.

I usually did higher level thinking, researched with the model, and then went to the implementation phase. But lately, I am not happy with both the research results (I continuesly have to narrow it down, go back, refine... I spend a day or 2 days refining, which in the end, I can do by myself now and actually feel a sense of accomplishment). Even the implementation isn't all that great.

Maybe my bar for acceptable work is higher now, since these tools are not "magic" anymore. I think I gave them more leeway in the beginning because they wowed me. But now... not so much anymore. I even dread opening up Claude Code or Codex and I'd rather read and write code myself, and just give them smaller tasks, or once I nailed it down, I let a large chunk of code write by a model (because it "types" faster...).

Am I alone? I read a lot of think pieces, I have agents working on my private dedicated server to maintain my machine and set up my self-hosting services. But more and more, I'd rather.... do it myself again, be more precise, and use it as a workhorse instead of a thinking researcher.

title: Ask HN: What's a tool or visualization that you wish existed?
summary:
Context behind my Ask: I believe AI has made it much faster for me to turn an idea into something I can actually try. That, in turn, has made me want to get more ambitious and build tools people would keep using or visualizations they’d get happily sidetracked exploring. With so much new stuff coming out, “build something people want” in some ways feels harder than ever.

Many of my ideas start with something I’ve wished for myself or based on an observation or need of someone I know. E.g. I have started running road / trail races around NYC and want a calendar that shows which races I qualify for and when registration opens to help me with remembering to sign up before a race fills up and remembering when to start training and show up.

When was the last time you wished there were a tool for something or wanted to see a dataset mapped or compared in a particular way? Are there any "magic wand" things you've been excited by the idea of but haven't been able to build or are looking for inspiration in regards to? Oddly specific answers are welcome.
